messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John, a 55-year-old African man and painter, has been struggling with intense emotional distress since his wife's unexpected death six months ago. John’s life was forever altered when he received the devastating news that his beloved spouse had passed away due to sudden cardiac arrest while at work. Since then, John finds himself hyper-vigilant in various situations. The sound of an ambulance siren, a common occurrence in his neighborhood, immediately triggers a surge of anxiety and fear, making him feel as though he is back on the day when everything changed. This reaction has significantly impacted his ability to sleep peacefully at night. He often finds himself unable to relax, constantly aware that danger could lurk just beyond his home’s threshold. The constant tension in his body and the feeling of being perpetually on guard have made it difficult for him to fully engage with everyday activities. John's triggers are not limited to external stimuli; they also stem from his workplace environment. As a painter, he frequently encounters conversations about accidents and loss, which invariably lead to painful recollections of his wife’s passing. These discussions evoke such intense grief that he often feels overwhelmed by emotions, even without clear visual memories of the event itself. These triggers have intensified John's negative appraisals about himself and his life. He has come to believe that since losing his wife, he no longer understands who he is or what purpose he serves. This sense of identity loss exacerbates his feelings of isolation from others; he often feels as though he cannot connect with people in the same way anymore because they do not fully comprehend the depths of his grief. The intensity of these negative appraisals has created a feedback loop that further escalates John’s threat perceptions and memories. His belief that life is irreparably destroyed by trauma makes him hyper-aware of potential dangers, even when he is at home. This heightened sense of alertness keeps his body in a constant state of readiness for danger, which in turn reinforces the negative appraisals about himself and his future. Conversely, John’s distressing memories often bring on waves of grief that are so intense they can be experienced without any clear visual recollections. The emotional intensity of these moments is overwhelming, causing him to feel as though he is reliving the trauma all over again. This experience further isolates him from others and deepens his sense of loss. The interplay between John’s memories and triggers has created a complex web of reactions that perpetuate each other. Each time he hears an ambulance siren or engages in conversations about loss, it brings back the emotional pain of losing his wife. These reminders intensify his negative appraisals and heighten his sense of threat. Over the past months, John’s work performance has suffered as these symptoms have grown more severe. He often avoids social gatherings and struggles to maintain connections with colleagues due to his heightened anxiety and grief. His inability to cope effectively has strained his relationships with family members, leaving him feeling increasingly isolated. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that he could no longer bear the burden of these overwhelming emotions alone. While he hopes for a return to some sense of normalcy, what frightens him most is the fear of never finding peace and being trapped in this cycle of grief and anxiety forever.
